Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Gameplay 2.1 Deal 2.2 Play 2.3 Elimination 3 Variants 3.1 Dog's Life 3.2 Card Exchange Objective Stay in the game by winning at least 1 trick each round. Gameplay Deal The dealing player rotates clockwise with each hand. For the first hand, deal 7 cards to each player. This number decreases by 1 each hand, until 1. There is a trump for each hand. For the first hand, turn the next card face up and use its suit. From the second hand onwards, the player who won the most tricks last hand chooses the trump instead, unless there is a tie (in that case, use the first hand's method). Play The play begins with the player to the dealer's left, who leads the first card. The lead may be any suit. Play follows clockwise. Each player must follow the suit led, if they can. If not, they may play any other card in their hand. The player who has played the highest trump card, or if no trump was played, the highest card of the suit led, wins the trick. That player then leads to the next trick. Continue until all tricks have been played and won. Elimination If a player takes no tricks in a hand, they are eliminated from the game. When all but one player are eliminated, the game ends and the surviving player wins. Variants Dog's Life The first time when a player would be eliminated (by taking no tricks in a hand), they gain the "Dog's Life" instead. If several players are eliminated simultaneously, they all gain the Dog's Life. A player on a Dog's Life is only dealt one card in the next hand, which can be played on any trick. If a player on a Dog's Life manages to take a trick with their hand, they reenter the game and is dealt a normal hand starting from the next hand, as normal. If not, they are eliminated. Card Exchange After trumps are chosen but before the first trick is led, each player may discard 0-3 cards and redraw the same number of cards. [Rating: 3/10] Played an lot of this as a kid. Just dumb luck really but I didn't know at the time.

[Rating: 4/10] This is a bad version of Whist just due to rules ensuring that luck has too big of influence. I like the Knockout aspect actually but it comes down too much to luck on who wins in the end.    Suitable for Children

[Rating: 4/10] Knockout mechanic makes good deal worse than regular Whist. Does not seem to be a lot of strategy. Dog’s life is interesting, but got a bad card each time so could not make use of it. Did do pretty good time of getting my family familiar with trick-taking.

[Rating: 4/10] [thing=20525][/thing] is a traditional trick-taking card game that user a regular deck of cards. The ideia is that each round players will have less and less cards in hands, and each person who doesn't take a trick, is knock out of the game. Last one standing, wins!  [thing=20525][/thing] is mostly a luck affair, specially as the rounds go by, and players have less cards. You just hope to have the right cards to keep going and maybe, near the end, decide the trump and likely win.  [thing=20525][/thing] is far from good, but at least is quick to play, easy to teach, and play well with children 

[Rating: 5/10] I use this (very simple) game to teach players other trick-taking games, like Hearts, Oh Hell, or even Bridge.  The evening tends to end up being spent playing this though, for some reason.

[Rating: 5/10] A fun Whist variant suitable for children up to younger teens. It was a favourite game in the common room during my senior years in secondary school.

[Rating: 5/10] OK for teaching kids the basics of Whist but too much randomness and too many extra chances. Use this for teaching but move them on to the better whist games quickly.

[Rating: 5/10] Not an exciting or challenging card game but quick and OK fun. We use old pennies as buy in tokens. Get's quite competitive
